title: Cleft and pseudo-cleft sentences
objectives: Identify the focused element in a cleft.
Form it-clefts and what-clefts with appropriate clause order.
Select a cleft for a specified contrast.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: A cleft sentence divides a message into two clauses to highlight one part of it. Compare “Maya found the key” with “It was Maya who found the key.” The second version presents Maya as the focused element: it is particularly useful when correcting the idea that someone else found it. The event remains the same, but the sentence guides the listener towards a different point of contrast.

A pseudo-cleft also divides information, usually beginning with a what-clause: “What we need is a quieter room.” This can introduce a need before naming the solution. Such structures are useful when the context makes the focus relevant; they can sound unnecessarily elaborate if every sentence uses them.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: An it-cleft often has it plus be, a focused element, and a clause introduced by who or that: “It was the guide who found the route” or “It was the route that the guide found.” Who is common for people; that can refer to people or things in many it-clefts. The choice of tense in be reflects the intended time, as in “It is the cost that concerns us.”

A common pseudo-cleft consists of a what-clause, be, and the focused information: “What she wanted was a break.” The what-clause is generally treated as singular in examples such as “What matters is the result”. When the complement is plural, usage can vary: both “What we need is more chairs” and “What we need are more chairs” occur.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Suppose two reports reached the director, but only the second prompted a response. “It was the second report that prompted the response” identifies the relevant report. To contrast the time, a writer might say “It was on Tuesday that the director responded.” In both cases, the clause following the focus helps identify the event being discussed.

In a meeting, “What I suggest is a short break” sets up the proposal and then supplies it. “All we need is a signature” is a related focusing construction: all we need names a restricted requirement. The choice between a cleft and a simple sentence depends on what the listener already knows and what should be highlighted.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: A cleft can change the information structure without changing the basic event, but it can also suggest a contrast or exclusiveness that a simple sentence does not force. “It was Lea who called” is especially natural when the caller is in question; it need not state that nobody else ever called. Avoid treating every cleft as a strict logical claim of uniqueness.

Keep the parts grammatical: “It was the guide who found the route”, not “It was the guide who did found the route”. After did, a base form would be needed, but no did is necessary here. In a what-clause, retain the required subject and verb: “What we need is time”, not “What need we is time”.

examples.sentence: It was Maya who found the key.
It was the key that Maya found.
examples.note: The key is the focused object.

examples.sentence: It was on Tuesday that the director responded.
It is the cost that concerns us.
examples.note: The present-tense cleft highlights the cost.

examples.sentence: What we need is a quieter room.
examples.note: The what-clause introduces the need before its specification.

examples.sentence: What she wanted was a break.
examples.note: Was matches the past framing of the statement.

examples.sentence: All we need is a signature.
examples.note: The construction focuses a restricted requirement.
The simple sentence is natural when no special contrast is needed.

common_errors.incorrect: It was Maya who did found the key.
common_errors.correct: It was Maya who found the key.
common_errors.reason: The relative clause does not need did here.

common_errors.incorrect: What need we is more time.
common_errors.correct: What we need is more time.
common_errors.reason: The what-clause has statement word order.

common_errors.incorrect: It was the key that Maya find yesterday.
common_errors.correct: It was the key that Maya found yesterday.
common_errors.reason: The past event takes found in the clause.

summary: An it-cleft highlights an element in a divided sentence.
A what-cleft can introduce a category before identifying its content.
Use these structures when their focus serves the surrounding discourse.

exercises.prompt: Choose the cleft that focuses the person who found the key.
exercises.explanation: Maya is the focused person after it was.

options.text: It was the key who Maya found.
What Maya was found the key.
It Maya who was found the key.
It was Maya who found the key.

option_feedback.a: “It was the key who Maya found.” does not fit here. Maya is the focused person after it was.
option_feedback.b: “What Maya was found the key.” does not fit here. Maya is the focused person after it was.
option_feedback.c: “It Maya who was found the key.” does not fit here. Maya is the focused person after it was.
option_feedback.d: “It was Maya who found the key.” fits here. Maya is the focused person after it was.

option_feedback.d: “What was Maya found the key.” does not fit here. The key appears in the focused position after it was.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence focuses the time of the response?
exercises.explanation: On Tuesday occupies the focused position in the it-cleft.

options.text: It was the director who responded on Tuesday.
It was on Tuesday that the director responded.
What the director did was respond.
The director responded on Tuesday.

option_feedback.a: “It was the director who responded on Tuesday.” does not fit here. On Tuesday occupies the focused position in the it-cleft.
option_feedback.b: “It was on Tuesday that the director responded.” fits here. On Tuesday occupies the focused position in the it-cleft.
option_feedback.c: “What the director did was respond.” does not fit here. On Tuesday occupies the focused position in the it-cleft.
option_feedback.d: “The director responded on Tuesday.” does not fit here. On Tuesday occupies the focused position in the it-cleft.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence has normal order inside the what-clause?
exercises.explanation: The embedded what-clause uses statement order: we need.

options.text: What need we is a break.
What do we need is a break.
What we need is a break.
What we do need is a break is.

option_feedback.a: “What need we is a break.” does not fit here. The embedded what-clause uses statement order: we need.
option_feedback.b: “What do we need is a break.” does not fit here. The embedded what-clause uses statement order: we need.
option_feedback.c: “What we need is a break.” fits here. The embedded what-clause uses statement order: we need.
option_feedback.d: “What we do need is a break is.” does not fit here. The embedded what-clause uses statement order: we need.

exercises.explanation: Who introduces the clause about the focused person.

exercises.explanation: That introduces the clause about the focused thing.

exercises.explanation: Is links the what-clause to the focused complement.

exercises.explanation: Was matches this past framing.

exercises.explanation: Was forms the past it-cleft.

exercises.explanation: The subject I takes the base form suggest.

exercises.prompt: All we ___ is a signature. (need)
exercises.explanation: We takes the base verb need.

exercises.explanation: Found is the past form of find.
